title: Minimal stable request envelope and compatibility playbook
summary: A focused, pragmatic proposal for a minimal, stable request envelope plus an operational compatibility playbook. Covers version negotiation, field stability guarantees, a small error-code taxonomy mapped to retry semantics, and explicit KV cache and kernel-scheduler interactions to guide runtime behavior and client fallbacks.
content:
Purpose
This note is intended as a compact, operationally-minded reference for the runtime API envelope and compatibility guarantees. It is not a full specification of all features; instead it prescribes a minimal stable surface we guarantee to clients, plus rules for rolling out changes, and how the request envelope should express KV/caching and kernel hints so the scheduler can make safe decisions.

Goals
- Define the smallest set of request fields we promise to keep stable (backwards/forwards) for N months.
- Provide clear handshake/negotiation semantics for clients and the control plane.
- Establish a concise error taxonomy mapped to retryability and suggested client behavior.
- Describe the required KV cache semantics (namespaces, keys, eviction hints) and how those influence kernel/scheduler decisions.
- Give a rollout checklist and automated tests for backward compatibility.

Minimal stable envelope (example)
This is the recommended minimal envelope we will guarantee across minor runtime releases (90-day notice for changes):

{
  "protocol_version": "1",            // integer string for cheap evolution
  "request_id": "uuid-v4",         // idempotency + logs correlation
  "client": {
    "id": "string",               // optional, used for quotas/metrics
    "capabilities": ["streams", "function-calls"] // optional list
  },
  "model": {
    "name": "gptx-16k",
    "variant": "fp16"              // optional, runtime may ignore if unsupported
  },
  "input": {
    "type": "text",               // text | embeddings | chat | binary
    "payload": "..."
  },
  "limits": {
    "max_tokens": 1024,
    "timeout_ms": 3000
  },
  "kv": {
    "namespace": "customer-123",   // stable: string namespace, used for isolation
    "key_prefix": "session-a/turn-", // recommended prefix semantics
    "intent": "warm",            // warm | no-cache | invalidate; hint to scheduler
    "consistency": "best-effort"// best-effort | strong (strong not guaranteed for hosted)
  },
  "client_hints": {
    "latency_priority": "low",    // low | medium | high - scheduler hint only
    "quality_floor": "baseline"   // baseline | high - informs quant/kernel choice
  }
}

Notes on fields
- protocol_version: numeric-string. Major increases (1 -> 2) are breaking and require explicit negotiation. Minor changes are additive; we vow to tolerate unknown fields in clients.
- model.variant: runtime may select an equivalent model_variant; clients should treat variant as a preference (not a guarantee) unless pinned via an explicit pinned_model_id field.
- kv.namespace and key_prefix are stable names used for cache isolation. Runtimes must not share KV across namespaces.
- kv.intent: a hint only. "warm" means client expects cached prefixes to be useful; runtime may try to schedule on kernels that retain KV efficiently. "invalidate" is a request to evict matching prefixes; runtime should acknowledge invalidation in the response.

Compatibility guarantees (playbook)
1) Backwards compatibility: For the life of protocol_version=1, we guarantee parsing and honoring of the minimal stable envelope fields above. Unknown/additional fields will be ignored.
2) Forward compatibility: Clients may include optional hints (client_hints) and the runtime may ignore unknown hints. If a runtime starts returning new output fields, clients should ignore unknown fields.
3) Deprecation: Deprecation of stable fields requires:
   - At least 90 days public notice,
   - A migration guide and automated client-side lint rules,
   - A compatibility test run (see testing checklist),
   - Opt-in flag on the server for the first 30 days ("deprecated-fields-allowed": true)
4) Breaking changes: require major protocol bump. We will publish a migration plan, a feature-flagged rollout, and automated conversion tooling where reasonable.

Handshake / negotiation flow (recommended)
1) Optional capability probe (lightweight): clients can issue a GET /v1/capabilities?client_version=1 which returns supported protocol_version range, supported model families, and kernel feature flags (e.g., kv-prefix-eviction, continuous-batching). This call is cached by clients for 5-60s.
2) If protocol mismatch (client.protocol_version > server.max_supported), client can try a fallback path or surface an upgrade error.
3) If client pins a model_variant not available, runtime responds with MODEL_VARIANT_UNAVAILABLE (see error codes) and a list of compatible variants (if any).

Error taxonomy (compact)
We provide a small set of error codes mapped to HTTP semantics and retry guidance. Clients should not parse message strings — use code field.

- RTE_1000: CLIENT_BAD_REQUEST — HTTP 400. Non-retryable. Examples: malformed JSON, missing request_id, illegal kv.namespace format.
- RTE_1100: CLIENT_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL — HTTP 426. Non-retryable. Client must downgrade protocol or upgrade.
- RTE_1200: CLIENT_PINNED_MODEL_NOT_FOUND — HTTP 404. Non-retryable; server may include "compatible_variants" array.

- RTE_2000: RUNTIME_OVERLOADED — HTTP 503. Retryable with backoff. When overloaded, runtime may include "deadline_ms" or "estimated_backoff_ms" in metadata.
- RTE_2100: KERNEL_SWITCH_REQUIRED — HTTP 202 (accepted). Indicates request accepted but will be processed on a different kernel than requested; response will include "expected_latency_ms". Retryable if client wants different latency/quality tradeoff.
- RTE_2200: KV_WARMUP_REQUIRED — HTTP 202. Processing deferred until KV prefix is warmed; response includes "warmup_handle" token. Client may choose to retry or wait via an async poll.

- RTE_3000: INTERNAL_EXECUTION_FAILURE — HTTP 500. Usually non-deterministic. Retryable once.
- RTE_3100: INCOMPATIBLE_KERNEL_CONFIG — HTTP 409. Non-retryable without changing request hints (quality_floor/latency_priority).

Guidelines for client retries
- 4xx codes: do not retry (fix request).
- 5xx and 503: exponential backoff, cap at 10s; respect Retry-After if present.
- 202 responses that include warmup_handle: client may either poll or request a degraded quality/low-latency path to avoid warmup.

KV cache semantics and scheduler implications
- Namespaces: KV is partitioned by kv.namespace. Runtimes must enforce isolation; namespace collisions are a client error.
- Keys: key_prefix must be a string token. Runtime computes full cache keys by concatenating key_prefix + client-provided suffix (if any). Clients should avoid including PII in keys.
- Consistency: Hosted API exposes only best-effort caching. Private deployments may opt into "strong" consistency mode via a deployment flag; strong mode has higher latency on invalidations.
- Eviction hints: kv.intent="invalidate" should be used for explicit invalidation. Runtimes guarantee best-effort eviction within the same namespace within 5s for hosted clusters (configurable in Dedicated).
- Hotness signals: runtime tracks prefix hit rates per kernel pool. Scheduler uses hotness to decide kernel placement: kernels with persistent KV retention (e.g., shard-local caches) get preference for "warm" intent and high hit-rate prefixes.

How kernel selection uses envelope hints (examples)
- If client_hints.latency_priority="high" and kv.intent="no-cache", scheduler favors low-latency kernels (small batch, on-demand).
- If kv.intent="warm" and prefix hit rate > 20% and client requests high throughput, schedule on batch-optimized kernels that keep KV pinned.
- If quality_floor="high" but requested model.variant is quantized only, scheduler can return RTE_3100 (INCOMPATIBLE_KERNEL_CONFIG) and offer backoff choices.

Fallback patterns and progressive degraded responses
1) Quality degrade: if model variant not available, runtime can deliver a lower-quality variant with explicit meta: "fallback_from" and "quality_impact". This is preferred to outright rejection for non-critical applications.
2) Latency degrade: client_hints.low-latency path may be served by a shorter-context kernel returning partial results with a continuation token.
3) KV-related fallback: when KV warmup is required, runtime may (a) return a partial response from scratch, (b) return async handle, or (c) route to a fallback kernel without KV but with higher compute cost. The runtime must include "fallback_reason" and "expected_quality_drop_pct".

Testing checklist (compatibility safety net)
- Unit tests that deserialize unknown fields and ensure no exception thrown.
- Contract tests: round-trip the minimal stable envelope across releases (golden fixtures).
- Interop tests: simulate older clients with newer runtimes and vice-versa.
- Chaos tests: inject failures in KV invalidation and confirm documented best-effort behavior.
- Performance tests: assert kernel choices when kv.intent toggles between warm/no-cache over synthetic workloads.

Rollout and telemetry to enforce guarantees
- Telemetry fields: every request must log request_id, protocol_version, kv.namespace, kv.intent, kernel_pool_id, latency_ms, and error_code (if any).
- Compatibility dashboard: track number of clients using older protocol_version and number of requests using deprecated fields.
- Opt-in migration: expose an admin flag to allow deprecated fields for a specific customer/workload for a transition window.

Open questions / decisions to make
- Do we permit client-supplied full cache keys (not just prefixes)? (security/PII concern)
- Is strong consistency required for some enterprise customers in-hosted mode or always only a Private option?
- How do we price KV-heavy workloads (retain per-prefix memory accounting)?

Action items
- (Maya) Draft a small JSON Schema for the minimal envelope and land it in runtime/protos.
- (Ethan) Add unit tests for unknown-field tolerance in the deserializer.
- (Priya) Create a Confluence migration timeline and customer communication templates.
- (Tom) Prototype telemetry dashboards tracking kv.intent vs kernel decisions.

Appendix: example error response (compact)
{
  "code": "RTE_2200",
  "http_status": 202,
  "message": "KV warmup required for prefix session-a/turn-7",
  "metadata": ["warmup_handle:abc123"]
}

(Do not rely on message strings; clients should parse code and metadata tokens.)

Concluding note
This playbook is intentionally narrow: pick a small set of stable fields and behavior guarantees we can operationalize. The next steps are to translate the minimal envelope to a JSON Schema and a set of unit/integration tests that run automatically during CI.

-- Maya
